title: Court holds N.L. man over fear he will commit terrorist acts after threats against mosque
summary: Facing eight charges and a court application used when there is a “fear of terrorism offence,” Matthew Collins was allegedly making threats against a mosque.

image.caption: Matthew Collins appeared by video in Gander provincial court Monday, Nov. 23. (Troy Turner/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Facing eight charges and a court application used when there is a “fear of terrorism offence,” Matthew Collins was allegedly making threats against a mosque.
Collins accused of making bomb, remains in custody
Police say a Gander resident facing charges related to threats, hate and explosives is accused of making a threat against a mosque.

"The RCMP takes seriously any threats that undermine an individual’s sense of safety and security," the RCMP said in a statement on Monday. "Violent statements will not be tolerated, and we will continue to enforce the recently added Criminal Code provisions addressing hate-motivated offences."
The RCMP statement comes on the heels of the arrest of last week’s arrest of Matthew Collins.
Collins, also known as Maddie, remains in custody awaiting a bail hearing.
Collins is facing eight charges including ones related to possessing explosives, uttering threats and intimidation "regarding a religious property," the RCMP said.
There was also a court application filed that is used when there is a "fear of terrorism offence."

items: Gander resident Matthew Collins faces charges related to alleged bomb making

blocks.text: Collins appeared in Gander provincial court by video Monday after being transported to St. John’s for medical attention over the weekend.
The appointment was arranged Friday, when duty counsel cited fears Collins would self-harm.
The court heard today that, for "medical and safety" reasons, Collins was unable to travel back to Gander.

A social media account under Collins' name and likeness features several anti-Islamic posts, videos using knives as weapons, and images such as this one, showing a household drone attached to a small missile-shaped object. (Facebook)

The investigation into Collins began on Monday, Nov. 16, when the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary contacted the Gander RCMP for assistance in locating someone who was posting online content and alleged threats toward a mosque.
Collins’s apartment was searched and police seized electronic devices and other evidence relevant to the investigation.
"Police officers had reasonable grounds to fear that Collins may commit terrorism offences," Monday’s statement from the RCMP stated.
Terrorism expert Lorne Dawson says no judge wants to be the person who declines a terrorism peace bond. (CBC)
A ‘distinguishing’ feature in Canadian law, says professor
Lorne Dawson is a professor emeritus at the University of Waterloo specializing in terrorism.
He also co-founded the Canadian Network for Research on Terrorism, Security and Society.
He says the application before the court is similar to a peace bond and has been used in Canada many times by courts looking to restrict conditions placed on an accused.
"It's actually one of the distinguishing features in Canada, because a lot of the jurisdictions around the world don't happen to have a similar legal avenue on the books," Dawson said.
Dawson has done extensive research within communities dealing with radicalization.
He said these applications were common after the defeat of the Islamic state in Syria and Iraq in 2019.

"We had all kinds of individuals coming back to Canada or being brought back by the Canadian government," he said. "We're mainly talking about … Canadian women who married ISIS fighters or Islamic State fighters were in the camps and they had children, and they were brought back to Canada. Almost all of them were placed on peace bonds."
Gander resident remains in custody awaiting bail as terrorism risk is assessed

In recent years, he said the frequency of the bonds has declined, but they are still prevalent throughout the country. In many cases, Dawson said the bonds find their way to court following investigations into online activity of the perpetrators.

"I would think the most strong evidence presented is usually going to be people's online activity," he said. "It's pretty easy to gather this with the sophisticated abilities available for the Canadian security establishment."
Dawson says authorities must still document information relating to the investigation into why there is a fear of terrorism, and must document their suspicions.
In his experience, judges impose peace bonds to try to prevent future crimes.

"The fear of a terrorist attack is so strong, and the jeopardy to the public is so great — and there are so many unknown variables that may precipitate a terrorist attack — that they revert to these bonds," he said.
"No judge wants to be the person that declined the peace bond, and then the individual goes ahead and perpetrates a terrorist offence."
Matthew Collins appears in Gander provincial court on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. (Troy Turner/CBC)
The peace bond application won’t be heard until after a decision on bail.
Collins’ next appearance is Wednesday in Gander provincial court.
Charges against Collins include:

items: Possessing explosive with intent to endanger life or damage property.
Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.
Uttering threats to damage or destroy property.
Intimidation by using or threatening violence.
